The Chariot ("Because I could not stop for Death")
by Emily Dickinson
The following poem is by Emily Dickinson (1890).

```passage
Because I could not stop for Death,
He kindly stopped for me;
The carriage held but just ourselves
And Immortality.

We slowly drove, he knew no haste,
And I had put away
My labor, and my leisure too,
For his civility.

We passed the school where children played,
Their lessons scarcely done;
We passed the fields of gazing grain,
We passed the setting sun.

We paused before a house that seemed
A swelling of the ground;
The roof was scarcely visible,
The cornice but a mound.

Since then 't is centuries; but each
Feels shorter than the day
I first surmised the horses' heads
Were toward eternity.
```

text_map.central_idea: Speaking from centuries after her death, the speaker remembers dying as a polite, unhurried carriage ride with a courteous Death. The ride passes images of a whole life and stops at a grave described as a sunken house. Only at the end does she reveal that she slowly realized the ride led to eternity. The calm, mannerly surface keeps death's finality half-hidden until the last stanza.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A first-person speaker who has died. She looks back from an eternity that has lasted 'centuries' to the day Death called for her. She was Death's passenger and, in effect, the woman he was courting.

We Wear the Mask
by Paul Laurence Dunbar
The following poem is by Paul Laurence Dunbar (1896).

```passage
We wear the mask that grins and lies,
It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,--
This debt we pay to human guile;
With torn and bleeding hearts we smile,
And mouth with myriad subtleties.

Why should the world be over-wise,
In counting all our tears and sighs?
Nay, let them only see us, while
    We wear the mask.

We smile, but, O great Christ, our cries
To thee from tortured souls arise.
We sing, but oh the clay is vile
Beneath our feet, and long the mile;
But let the world dream otherwise,
    We wear the mask!
```

text_map.central_idea: A collective speaker describes a smiling mask that a suffering group wears before an observing world. The poem presents the mask as a debt forced on the group and also as a chosen guard over their private grief. Only in the cry to Christ does the speaker name the anguish beneath it, and the poem then ends by declaring the mask again.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A first-person plural voice ('we') speaking for a group that hides its suffering from 'the world'. In the third stanza the voice turns from the world and speaks directly to Christ.

    Little Mrs. Sommers one day found herself the
unexpected possessor of fifteen dollars. It seemed to
her a very large amount of money, and the way in which
it stuffed and bulged her worn old porte-monnaie gave
her a feeling of importance such as she had not enjoyed
for years.

    The question of investment was one that occupied her
greatly. For a day or two she walked about apparently in
a dreamy state, but really absorbed in speculation and
calculation. She did not wish to act hastily, to do
anything she might afterward regret. But it was during
the still hours of the night when she lay awake
revolving plans in her mind that she seemed to see her
way clearly toward a proper and judicious use of the
money.

    A dollar or two should be added to the price usually
paid for Janie’s shoes, which would insure their lasting
an appreciable time longer than they usually did. She
would buy so and so many yards of percale for new shirt
waists for the boys and Janie and Mag. She had intended
to make the old ones do by skilful patching. Mag should
have another gown. She had seen some beautiful patterns,

stanzas: Little Mrs. Sommers one day found herself the

options.why: The plans are all for the children, but once she is tired and unfed she yields to the tempting, serpent-like silk.
options.label: correct

options.text: The passage portrays Mrs. Sommers as a shrewd bargain hunter whose skill at the counter defines her whole identity and worth.
options.why: She is a skilled bargain hunter, but she is defined chiefly by her family's needs and by the passage's turn toward desire.
options.label: partially_right

options.text: The passage mocks Mrs. Sommers's nostalgia for her former better days, exposing her vanity as the true source of her poverty.
options.why: She refuses to dwell on the past, and nothing in the passage blames vanity for her poverty.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The passage argues that all poverty inevitably corrupts the moral character of every person who must endure it for many long, weary years.
options.why: This makes a sweeping claim about everyone. Mrs. Sommers is shown as careful and conscientious.
options.label: too_broad

"The passage argues that all poverty inevitably corrupts the moral character of every person who must endure it for many long, weary years." is incorrect: This makes a sweeping claim about everyone. Mrs. Sommers is shown as careful and conscientious.
